faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Oakland chimney?
faqs.a: Yes — spring raccoon mothers choose uncapped chimneys across Garrett County. Our crew checks whether pups are present before anything moves, removes the family together whenever we can, and fits a proper chimney cap so the same chimney is not a den again next spring.

faqs.q: When is wildlife pressure worst in Oakland?
faqs.a: Spring denning and the fall push indoors are the two busy waves in Garrett County, with bat colonies and mole damage peaking in summer. If you are hearing noise or seeing digging in Oakland, calling at the first sign almost always makes for a simpler, cheaper job.

faqs.q: Our Mt. Lake Park cottage sits empty all winter. How do we keep raccoons and bats out of it?
faqs.a: Vacancy is the whole problem — an undisturbed house is a den waiting to be claimed. The durable fix is a full seal done while you are here: chimney capped, soffit and eave gaps closed in metal, foundation vents screened, and any existing colony or den excluded first. We also walk the attic for the season's worth of droppings and nesting so you are not opening in spring to a cleanup bill. Homes sealed this way in the fall come through the winter quiet; homes that just get a trap visit do not.

faqs.q: A porcupine is chewing the trim on our cabin. Is that something you handle?
faqs.a: Porcupines are part of life in the Savage River woods — they gnaw wood, siding, and even tool handles for the salt and the wood itself. We will assess what is drawing it (salt-treated wood and outbuildings are the usual targets), advise on removing the attractant and protecting the structure, and tell you plainly what can and cannot be done under Maryland rules. It is a call worth making before a cabin's trim and steps are gnawed through.

Oakland is a working mountain county seat, and its wildlife work looks different from the lake's. The Victorian and rail-era homes around the courthouse and the old B&O station have tall attics and layered rooflines where bats summer and squirrels chew in before the first real cold. Out along the Little Youghiogheny and the roads toward Mt. Lake Park, the big old summer-colony cottages — many opened only part of the year — are raccoon and bat houses: a home that sits closed and quiet for months is exactly what a denning animal is looking for, and the homeowner often discovers a whole season of damage in a single weekend.

Winter drives the rest of our Oakland calendar. Garrett County is Maryland's high plateau, the coldest, snowiest corner of the state, and animals here push into structures earlier and harder than anywhere else we work. Groundhogs dig under the farm outbuildings and the stone foundations outside town, skunks take the crawlspaces in town, and porcupines — common in the Savage River woods — occasionally turn up gnawing the siding and trim of outlying cabins, a call you almost never hear downstate. Our fall sealing runs in Oakland are booked by people who learned the year before what a February raccoon in the attic costs.
Oakland.extendedBody:
Rail-era roofs and summer-colony cottages

Oakland's older stock was built for coal smoke and mountain winters, not for keeping animals out. Decorative eaves and a century of re-roofing leave gaps at every junction, chimneys in the downtown blocks have stood uncapped for decades, and the Mt. Lake Park cottages add a second problem: long vacancy. A cottage closed from October to May gives a raccoon or a bat colony an undisturbed season, and guano and nesting accumulate where nobody sees them. Our inspections of those homes start in the attic and work outward, because by the time the owner arrives, the entry point is the least of the findings — the cleanup is the job.

How our work is permitted in Garrett County

Every job is handled by a Maryland DNR-licensed Wildlife Damage Control Operator, which is the permit Maryland requires for commercial nuisance work. Maryland's rules draw a hard line on rabies-vector species — raccoons, skunks, and foxes may not be relocated, full stop — so our answer for those animals is exclusion and sealing: get them out, close the entry, and make the structure useless to the next one. That is not a limitation on the work; it is why the work lasts.

Reading an Oakland property

We check the roofline and chimney, then the stone or block foundation for ground-level digs, then porches, decks, and outbuildings — in farm country the barn and the woodpile are usually part of the same animal's route. Porcupine sign (gnawed trim, stripped bark on nearby trees) and bear sign get pointed out when we see them, with straight guidance on who handles what, because pretending every problem is a trapping job does nobody in Garrett County any good.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Grantsville porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside at dusk and do not try to block the opening while the skunk is home — that traps it and guarantees a spray. Our crew removes skunks from under porches and decks in Grantsville with covered, low-stress handling, then screens the opening so the next skunk cannot move in.

faqs.q: Are bats a problem in Grantsville homes?
faqs.a: Yes — older rooflines and quiet attics in Grantsville host summer colonies, and in Garrett County the work is exclusion only, timed around the maternity season. Our crew maps every entry, fits one-way exits in the right window, and seals the building behind the bats.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my McHenry attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night-only scratching in Garrett County often means bats, flying squirrels or raccoons, while daytime running usually points to gray squirrels. Around Savage River State Forest, the cover close to housing means several species are plausible, so call us for an inspection and we will identify the animal before anything is sealed.

faqs.q: We found bats in our Deep Creek rental between guests. How fast can this be handled?
faqs.a: Call us as soon as you find it — a bat in the living space of a rental is a same-day conversation, both for the guests and for the health guidance that goes with it. The colony itself is handled by exclusion: entries mapped, secondary gaps sealed, one-way exits fitted so the bats leave on their own. Timing follows the season and whether flightless young are present, and we will tell you exactly what can happen this week versus what gets scheduled, plus how to document it for your rental listing.

faqs.q: Our lake house is empty most of the winter. What is the one thing that prevents spring surprises?
faqs.a: A full seal done in the fall, before the house goes quiet. Raccoons and bats claim empty houses over the winter precisely because nothing disturbs them; a capped chimney, screened vents, and metal-closed soffit gaps mean the house that gets checked in April is the house you left in October. We inspect, exclude anything already in residence, seal, and clean the attic so the first spring visit is a visit, not a discovery.

McHenry is Deep Creek Lake's front door, and its wildlife problem is the vacation-home problem at full scale. Hundreds of lake houses, chalets, and rental properties around the coves sit empty between visits — sometimes between rental groups, sometimes from October to ski season — and a quiet house on a wooded lot above the water is the single most attractive den site in Garrett County. Bats take the high A-frame roof peaks and the chimney chases of the chalets, raccoons move into attics and under lake-side decks, and by the time an owner or a rental guest reports it, the animals have usually been there a while.

The shore itself feeds the pressure. Deep Creek's wooded coves, the state park shoreline, and the streams running down to the lake keep raccoons, skunks, and squirrels in constant motion past every dock and deck, while Wisp's slopes and the surrounding forest hold the groundhogs that burrow under outbuildings and retaining walls on the hillside lots. Our McHenry work is built around the reality of these homes: inspections that fit between rental turns, sealing done to hold while nobody is there to notice a problem starting, and cleanup that leaves a house ready for guests, not just empty of animals.
McHenry.extendedBody:
The empty-house problem on Deep Creek Lake

A primary home reports its wildlife early — somebody hears the attic noise the first night. A vacation home reports it months late, and the difference shows up as guano depth, insulation damage, and smells that have soaked into a rental property's reviews. That is why our McHenry inspections assume occupation until proven otherwise: attic, chimney chase, the voids under lake-side decks, and the crawlspaces of the older lake cottages all get opened or scoped. Chalets deserve a special note — their tall framed peaks and decorative ridge vents are bat architecture, and sealing them takes lift work and patience, not a tube of foam.

Sealing that has to hold while nobody's home

Every job is run by a Maryland DNR-licensed Wildlife Damage Control Operator. Because Maryland prohibits relocating rabies-vector species — raccoons and skunks among them — the work here is exclusion and armouring: one-way exits for the animals in residence, then every entry closed in materials that survive a winter of nobody watching. For rental properties we also document what was found and fixed, so an owner managing from three hours away has a record, not just a bill.

Shoreline, slopes, and the lots between

Groundhogs burrow the sunny banks above the lake and under outbuilding slabs; skunks den under hot-tub decks and lake-side porches; squirrels run the canopy over the older cottage roads. We read the whole lot on a McHenry call — house, deck, dock structures, and outbuildings — because on a wooded lake lot the animals treat all of it as one address, and sealing only the house just moves the problem twenty feet.
